passage: Everyone in Class 9 knew me: I'm the boy who lends pens and carries the cricket kit. When the captain election was announced, I told myself the votes were already mine. I made no poster and wrote no speech, and on nomination day I skipped the class visits to play cricket. Gurleen, my rival, went from room to room with a two-line promise about a working water cooler and a library corner, and she even visited the Class 6 and 7 rows, which I had never thought of. On result day my friends were shocked. I lost by forty votes. I sat on the steps thinking: they liked me, but nobody knew what I would do. I'm Sandeep, and I have not forgotten that feeling.

qa.q: By how many votes did Sandeep lose?
What was Sandeep feeling on the steps, and what did the loss show?
qa.a: Sandeep felt shocked and let down, and saw that being liked was not enough because nobody knew what Sandeep would do.

qa.q: What could Sandeep have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Sandeep could have visited every class with one clear proposal and asked what students needed, because votes follow a plan people can picture.

qa.q: How might a Class 7 student have seen the two candidates?
qa.a: A Class 7 student would have seen Gurleen visit and speak clearly, while Sandeep never came, so Gurleen would seem the more serious choice.

grounding: A well-liked student assumes friends will vote for them and makes no plan, and rivals with clear proposals reach more classes, so the student loses despite a lot of goodwill.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B, after the house captain election

Akash is one of the most liked students in this class. For the two weeks of the campaign, he told me more than once, "Ma'am, everyone's my friend, it's sorted." I did not see him make a poster or visit any class except ours.

His rival, Neelam, visited all eleven sections with a one-page list: a lost-and-found box, fixed fans in the Class 6 rooms, and a monthly house quiz. Juniors stopped me in the corridor to ask about her quiz.

Akash lost by forty votes. At dispersal he sat on the bench long after the others had left, turning his badge over and over.

I sat beside him and asked what he had learned. He said, "Being liked isn't a plan." I have asked him to help Neelam run the house quiz.

qa.q: How many sections did Neelam visit?
qa.a: Neelam visited all eleven sections with a one-page list.

qa.q: What might Akash have been feeling as he turned his badge over on the bench?
qa.a: He was probably stunned and disappointed, perhaps a little ashamed, having been so sure his popularity would win.

qa.q: What approach could Akash have used instead of relying on being liked?
qa.a: He could have visited other classes and offered two or three concrete ideas, since juniors were clearly drawn to specific proposals like the quiz.

qa.q: How might the juniors in other sections have seen the two candidates?
qa.a: To them Neelam was a real person with a plan who came to their room, while Akash was mostly a name they had not heard from.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a well-liked student making no plan and losing to a rival with clear proposals who reached more classes.

passage:
Thursday night

I lost. To Aditi. By a lot.

I keep replaying it. Last month I honestly thought the election was a formality. Half the school says hi to me in the corridor. The cricket team, the drama lot, my whole tuition batch. I didn't make a single poster because what's the point, everyone knows me.

Aditi went to every class with a sheet about the broken drinking taps and a plan for a book swap. She even talked to the Class 6 kids nobody bothers with.

Today in the hall I heard juniors say, "Aditi came to our class, she explained everything." Nobody said my name like that.

It stings. People like me, but they didn't know what I'd actually do. I'm Raghav, the guy with lots of friends and no plan. Next year I'm writing things down.

qa.q: What did Aditi's sheet talk about?
qa.a: Aditi's sheet was about the broken drinking taps and a plan for a book swap.

qa.q: How is Raghav feeling on Thursday night?
qa.a: Raghav feels stung and embarrassed, replaying the loss and realising the goodwill was not enough.

qa.q: What would you advise Raghav to change first for next year?
qa.a: Start by visiting other classes and asking what bothers them, then build two or three written proposals, because friends' goodwill is not a platform.

qa.q: How might Aditi see her win?
qa.a: Aditi might feel proud and rewarded, since the win came from hard work visiting every class, including the Class 6 kids nobody bothers with.

grounding: A diary shows a well-liked student making no plan, losing to a rival with clear proposals who talked to more classes.
